procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge (PMLA cases) Jaipur, where Prosecution complaint no. 12/2018 in ECIR No.JPZO/01/2016 was pending.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The common judgment and order dated 21.02.2019 passed by the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at Jaipur, in S.B. Criminal Writ Petition No. 704 of 2018 and S.B. Criminal Writ Petition No. 757 of 2018.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court dismissed S.B. Criminal Writ Petition No. 704 of 2018 and S.B. Criminal Writ Petition No. 757 of 2018, imposing a cost of Rs. 50,000/-.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioners approached the Supreme Court by way of Special Leave Petitions (Crl.) Nos. 2397-2398 of 2019 challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated 21.02.2019. They sought to quash the High Court's judgment and order and stay the proceedings of the prosecution complaint pending before the Special Judge. The Supreme Court dismissed the petitions and vacated the interim relief granted earlier.

directions: The interim relief granted earlier stands vacated forthwith.

It is needless to say that the observations made against the petitioners in this order are only prima facie and the trial court shall decide the case on merits without being influenced by the said observations.
The E.D shall be at liberty to proceed further with the Prosecution complaint in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the criminal proceedings initiated by the Enforcement Directorate against the petitioners should be quashed.

facts: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) filed a Prosecution Complaint against the petitioners, alleging their direct involvement in activities connected with the proceeds of crime.
The petitioners argued that the proceedings should be quashed because they were not named in the original FIR or the subsequent Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR).

They contended that a key element for the offense of money laundering, namely 'knowledge' of involvement with proceeds of crime, was missing, and therefore the continuation of proceedings was an abuse of the legal process.
The petitioners had previously challenged the proceedings in the High Court, which dismissed their petitions with costs.
law: The Court referenced the principle established in 'State of Haryana and Others. vs. Bhajan Lal and Others', which states that the power to quash a criminal complaint should only be exercised in the 'rarest of rare' cases.
According to this principle, a complaint can be quashed only where the allegations, taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute any offense.
application: The Court found that, contrary to the petitioners' claims, the complaint contained specific allegations of money laundering against them.
It determined that these allegations and the supporting material presented by the ED were sufficient to prima facie constitute an offense under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA).
Since the allegations on their face did suggest an offense, the case did not meet the high threshold of being a 'rarest of rare' case that would justify quashing the complaint.
The Court concluded that the material in the complaint was significant enough to require a full trial by the competent court to decide the case on its merits.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioners' request and dismissed their petitions. It held that the complaint contained sufficient allegations and material to establish a prima facie case of money laundering, which warranted a trial and did not meet the high standard required for quashing criminal proceedings.

cases.case_name: State of Haryana and Others v. Bhajan Lal and Others
cases.principle: Cited for the illustrative categories of cases where the extraordinary power under Article 226 of the Constitution or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be exercised to prevent abuse of the process of any court or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or the extraordinary power under Article 226 of the Constitution can be exercised to quash proceedings where there is an express legal bar to their institution and continuance under the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act.
obiter: Money laundering poses a serious threat to the financial system of the countries and to their integrity and sovereignty, and any lenient view in dealing with such offences would be a travesty of justice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The petitioners' case does not meet the stringent criteria required to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., as established in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal. The petitioners failed to demonstrate that their case falls into any of the illustrative categories for quashing, such as the allegations being absurd or the proceedings being instituted with mala fide intent. Furthermore, they did not make out a case of abuse of process by the respondent authorities, and there is sufficient material to establish a prima facie case of their involvement in the alleged offence of money laundering.
legal_tests_applied: The power to quash a complaint under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. should be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection, and that too in the rarest of rare cases, as guided by the principles in State of Haryana and Others v. Bhajan Lal and Others.

Whether the case falls into one of the illustrative categories where the power to quash can be exercised, such as: '(3) Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.', '(5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.', or '(7) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge.'
why_appellant_lost: The case of the petitioners does not fall under any of the above categories [from Bhajan Lal].
The petitioners have also failed to make out any case of abuse of process of the court at the instance of the respondent authorities.
why_respondent_won: There being enough material to show prima facie involvement of the petitioners in the alleged offence of money laundering, as contemplated under the PMLA.

direct involvement of the petitioners in the activities connected with the proceeds of crime has been alleged, along with the material narrated in the complaint which would require a trial to be conducted by the competent court.
policy_considerations: money laundering poses a serious threat not only to the financial systems of the countries but also to their integrity and sovereignty.
Hence any lenient view in dealing with such offences would be a travesty of justice.
